b.bio: Stephanus Alessandri appears in this library only as a one-page approval in PL 46, where he signs as a procurator general and apostolic delegate alongside Aloysius Belmonte, pro-chancellor. No surviving record gives biographical details for this man. He should not be confused with Alessandro Alessandri (1461–1523), the Neapolitan lawyer who wrote Genialium dierum libri sex, nor with Giovanni Mario Alessandri, the sixteenth-century grammarian, whose works are unrelated to what is held here.
b.s: His single page here is an ecclesiastical approval appended to another work, not an independent treatise.

b.bio: Sigebertus (Siwart) Haverkamp was born in Leeuwarden in December 1684 and died at Leiden in April 1742. One older source gives the birth year as 1683, but the Leeuwarden baptismal register places it in December 1684. He studied at Leiden, served first as a preacher in a small village, then was called to Leiden as professor of history and Greek. He published an edition of Tertullian's Apologeticus (Leiden, 1718), a translation of Josephus' complete works (Amsterdam, 1726), and Abudacnus' Historia Jacobitarum (Leiden, 1740); an edition of his Josephus was owned by Thomas Jefferson. The works held here are his editorial paratexts to patristic texts in Migne's Patrologia Latina.
b.s: The pieces here are the prefatory apparatus of a working textual critic: Haverkamp defends his new edition of Tertullian's Apologeticus against prior editors (Rigault, Prieur, Scaliger) by arguing from manuscript witnesses — the Fulda codex as best witness to the Apologeticum, two distinct Agobard codices, and ancient exemplars correcting corrupt printed texts.

b.bio: Sixtus Senensis (Sixtus of Siena), born at Siena in 1520, was a Jewish convert to Catholicism. He first joined the Franciscans, was condemned to death for heresy or recidivism in Rome, and was spared when Cardinal Michele Ghislieri (the future Pius V) secured his recantation and transfer to the Dominicans around 1551. He preached against Judaism in the synagogues of the Papal States and in April 1559 helped burn the Talmud at Cremona while sparing the Zohar. His principal work, the Bibliotheca Sancta (Venice, 1566), treats the authority and interpretation of Scripture and lists biblical interpreters.
b.s: He coined the term 'deuterocanonical' and fixed 'protocanonical' and 'apocryphal' as standard categories for the Old Testament books, and his Bibliotheca Sancta is counted the first modern-style introduction to Scripture.

b.bio: Francesco Scipione Maffei, born and died in Verona (1 June 1675 – 11 February 1755), was an Italian littérateur, dramatist, soldier, and archaeologist from an illustrious family originally of Bologna. He joined the Accademia degli Arcadi in Rome in 1699 and on his return established a Verona branch. In 1703 he enlisted in the Bavarian army and in 1704 took part in the battle near Donauwörth (Schellenberg). In 1709 he went to Padua, where he shared with Apostolo Zeno the editorship of the Giornale de' Letterati d'Italia. He declined posts offered by Pope Clement XI and King Victor Amadeus. His antiquarian publications on Etruscan antiquities are counted among the beginnings of Etruscology.
b.s: The works held here are not by a Church Father but by the eighteenth-century editor whose Verona edition of Zeno supplied the Prolegomena, Epistle, and Preface printed in PL 70 and PL 9; they defend his reconstruction of Verona's episcopal list and dating of Zeno against Ughelli, Baronius, and other compilers.

b.bio: Stefano Antonio Morcelli was born at Chiari near Brescia on 17 January 1737 and died there 1 January 1822. He was admitted into the Society of Jesus on 3 November 1753. He taught grammar at Fermo, humanities at Ragusa, and oratory at the Roman College, where he established an academy of archaeology at the Kircherian Museum. After the suppression of the Jesuits in 1773 he served as librarian to Cardinal Albani, then in 1791 was appointed to a provostship in his native town, declining the offer of the Archbishopric of Ragusa. He was chiefly an epigraphist: his De stilo inscriptionum latinarum (Rome, 1781) gave him European fame and is considered a milestone in the development of epigraphy. Among his numerous works was Africa Christiana (Brescia, 1816–17).
b.s: The work held here, the Annals of the African Church (PL 3), is a history of the early African church centred above all on Cyprian of Carthage, built from patristic citations and ancient historians; it argues against Novatian, Felicissimus, Stephen of Rome, Fidus, and Demetrianus, and cites Cyprian most heavily, along with Pontius, Augustine, Eusebius, and Jerome.

w: Preface to the edition of Peter Chrysologus

b.bio: Sebastian Paoli was born at Lucca in 1684; he entered the Order of the Mother of God, served as general procurator of the congregation from 1729, and was rector of the college of St. Brigitta at Naples, where he died in 1751. He was regarded as one of the most famous antiquarians of his time, writing on early Christian poetry and publishing a diplomatic codex of the military order of Jerusalem (Malta). He also published an edition of the Orations of Peter Chrysologus at Venice in 1750.
b.s: The work held here is his prefatory matter to an edition of Peter Chrysologus, arguing that printed editions are corrupt, that Chrysologus used the Itala text of Scripture, that spurious sermon titles should be erased entirely, that nine lessons were drawn from Agnellus's life, that the Bologna 1534 printing is the editio princeps, and that ancient codices must not be emended by private judgment.

b.bio: Suffridus Petri (Sjoerd Pieters), born in Leeuwarden on 15 June 1527 and died in Cologne on 23 January 1597, was a Frisian jurist, classical philologist and historian. After studies at Leuven from 1547 he became a licentiate of laws, librarian to Granvelle, professor of classical languages at Erfurt, and later professor of Greek and canon in Cologne. As historiographer for the States of Friesland he wrote De Frisiorum antiquitate et origine and De Scriptoribus Frisiae, a history mixing older tradition with legend and invention. The work held here is his prefatory matter to an edition printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 58.
b.s: The library holds only his preface in PL 58, not a patristic work of his own; readers should treat him as the learned editor whose front matter accompanies that volume rather than as one of the Latin Fathers.

w: Annals of the Deeds of Charlemagne

b.bio: An anonymous Saxon poet known only by this name, who wrote in the reign of Arnulf of Carinthia. He composed the Annales de gestis Caroli Magni imperatoris in five books (2,683 lines), books 1–4 in hexameters and book 5 on Charlemagne's death in elegiac distichs. He calls the Saxons 'our people' and drew chiefly on the Annales Einharti and Einhard's Vita Karoli; he was probably a monk of Saint Gall or possibly Corvey, and recent scholarship (Rembold) places the poem at Paderborn as part of a programme promoting episcopal authority there.
b.s: His poem is one of the earliest poetic treatments of annalistic material and one of the earliest historical works centered on Saxony, presenting Charlemagne's rule as divinely granted and the Saxons' conversion as deliverance from error.

b.bio: Salomon III, bishop of Constance, belonged to the episcopal dynasty that ruled that see until 919. Sources describe him as a liturgist and poet; Biblissima dates him c. 860–920. He should not be confused with his predecessor Solomon I (died 871), the first of the same dynasty. The library holds a single short set of verses from PL 132 (6 pages): brief poetic pieces on the Church, prayer, last things, and the civil magistrate, citing Gregory, Paul, Virgil, and Ovid alongside biblical exempla.
b.s: The verses here are minor Carolingian Latin poetry by a ruling bishop, useful chiefly as evidence of how biblical exempla and classical authors were turned to moral and ecclesiastical instruction in his circle.

b.bio: Secundinus (Irish Sechnall) was a fifth-century missionary bishop in Ireland, founder of Domhnach Sechnaill near Tara. Annalistic sources describe him as sent in aid of Patrick together with Auxilius and Iserninus; medieval tradition made him a disciple of Patrick and a bishop of Armagh, but historians regard that connection as possibly a later Armagh construction, and he may instead have been an independent missionary, perhaps linked to Palladius. The earliest historical references to him are in Tirechan's Collectanea. His death is variously dated c.447 or 457.
b.s: The works held here are two Latin hymns attributed to him, treating the Trinity (one substance in three persons), the church founded on Peter's confession, baptismal grace, apostolic mission, and the Christian life of chastity, prayer, good works, and glory in the cross.

b.bio: Secundinus was an African Manichaean known only as the author of a single letter to Augustine, written after Augustine had deserted the sect to which he was once attached. The letter gently upbraids him for leaving and urges his return in earnest, flattering terms, arguing from Scripture that sin lies in the free consent of the will, that unrepented rather than committed sin is punished, and that repentant apostasy can be healed by indulgent forgiveness. Augustine replied around AD 405 in Contra Secundinum Manichaeum, confuting the Manichaeans from his correspondent's own words. No source gives dates or further biographical details for Secundinus himself.
b.s: The library holds his Epistle to Augustine (in two Patrologia Latina printings, PL 42 and PL 20), one of the few surviving works written by a Manichaean to Augustine himself, valuable as direct evidence of Roman Manichaean 'biblical' argument in the age of Augustine.

b.bio: A Gallo-Roman bishop active in southern Gaul around the turn of the sixth century, and a correspondent of Ruricius of Limoges within the aristocratic episcopal network of Aquitaine and Septimania under Visigothic rule. He is generally identified with Sedatus of Nîmes, a bishop attested in the milieu of Caesarius of Arles and known for his theological learning; sermons have been transmitted under his name, including a Sermo in natale Domini transmitted as pseudo-Augustine sermon 117. Beyond this correspondence and a handful of conciliar and homiletic notices, the details of his career are sparsely documented.
b.s: The work held here is a two-page Epiphany homily reading Christ's baptism as done for sinners' sake, the six jars as six ages of the world whose measures signify trinitarian faith, the wine's failure as the law yielding to grace without perishing (the law progresses rather than perishes in Christ), the third day as pointing to resurrection, grace as an earnest with eternal life as dowry, and Christ as bridegroom joined to the church.

w: History of the Monastery of Chaumousey

b.bio: Seher of Chaumont (Seherus) was a solitary at the Châtelet who founded the abbey of Chaumouzey in the diocese of Toul and was blessed as its abbot by Bishop Pibo in 1094. He had long disputes with the abbey of Remiremont over jurisdiction and the status of canonesses there. His De primordiis Calmosiacensis monasterii is a history and cartulary of his abbey, preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 162). He is not to be confused with Henri Chaumont, the nineteenth-century Parisian priest and founder of the St. Francis de Sales societies.
b.s: His History of the Monastery of Chaumousey is a primary record of a Benedictine foundation's origins, its episcopal grants, and its conflicts with Remiremont.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author. Metellus of Tegernsee (fl. 1145–1165), a monk-poet of the abbey, is a different figure with a different name, and the fourteenth-century epic poet Seifrit is likewise someone else. What can be said comes from the library record alone: three pages of letters in PL 142 written from Tegernsee during a conflict over monastic office, in which an abbot defends obedience to his spiritual father, protests servitude imposed on his monks, and argues that an innocent abbot may ransom his office with church goods under compulsion.
b.s: The letters here are a first-hand record of an eleventh- or twelfth-century dispute between Tegernsee and the monastery of St. Emmeram involving imperial power over church offices.

b.bio: Sergius I was born to a Syrian family from Antioch settled at Palermo in Sicily. He came to Rome under Adeodatus II and was made cardinal-priest of Santa Susanna by Leo II on 27 June 683. Elected pope in December 687 after a disputed three-way election against the archdeacon Paschal and the archpriest Theodore, he reigned until his death on 8 September 701. His pontificate is marked by his refusal of the Quinisext (Trullan) canons of 692, which brought him into conflict with Emperor Justinian II, whose attempt to arrest him was thwarted; by his dealings with England, including the baptism of King Caedwalla (689) and the consecration of Willibrord for Frisia.
b.s: The two short texts held here — a letter to Abbot Ceolfrid holding that learned examination of disputed church questions profits the whole church, and a privilege anathematizing clerics who seize monastic cemetery rights or property — show the pope asserting papal authority over monastic obedience, property, and discipline.

b.bio: Sergius II was bishop of Rome from January 844 until his death on 27 January 847. A Roman noble educated in the schola cantorum, he was made cardinal-priest of Sts. Martin and Sylvester by Paschal I and archpriest under Gregory IV, whom he succeeded after a disputed election in which the populace briefly enthroned the deacon John as antipope; Sergius intervened to spare John's life. He was consecrated without awaiting imperial ratification required by the Constitutio Romana of 824; Emperor Lothair I sent his son Louis with an army, and the dispute ended in negotiation. His pontificate saw an Arab raid on Rome.
b.s: The epistle held here defends papal oversight of provincial synods and canonical discipline against interference by the Frankish kings Louis and Charles, asserting delegated vicarial authority, papal review of synodal decisions, and eternal punishment for schismatics and persecutors.

b.bio: Sergius III was a Roman of noble birth, son of Benedict, made bishop of Caere by Pope Formosus and a candidate for the papacy in 898 before being elected pope on 29 January 904, taking the throne from Antipope Christopher. His pontificate fell amid violent aristocratic faction-fighting in central Italy, with the Tusculan count Theophylact I influential behind him. He declared the ordinations conferred by Formosus null and continued the conflicts over Formosus' legacy; accusations that he murdered his two predecessors or fathered the future John XI are reported only by hostile or ill-informed sources and are doubtful.
b.s: The letters and privileges held here show his pontificate's practical side: confirming monastic electoral privileges, anathematizing their violation, ruling that a bishop may not leave his own see, and continuing the polemic against Formosus and his partisans such as King Arnulf, Archbishop Hermann of Cologne, and Hatto of Mainz.

b.bio: Sergius IV was born Pietro Martino Buccaporci in Rome, son of Peter the Shoemaker of the Pina district; his birth date is unknown. He became Cardinal-Bishop of Albano in 1004 and was elected pope on 31 July 1009 after the abdication of John XVIII, taking a new name on election — an early instance of what became customary. His temporal authority was eclipsed by the patrician John Crescentius, against whom he strengthened the pro-German party. The papyrus originals of some of his grants of privilege survive; several exempted monasteries from episcopal jurisdiction.
b.s: The letters and diplomas held here are papal privileges confirming and protecting church property: they assert that violation of papal privilege incurs anathema, that successors must confirm predecessors' grants, that tithes owed to God by testamentary command must not pass to laymen, that an archpriest's penitential judgment is limited by episcopal recourse, and that papal protection forbids seizure of granted property.

b.bio: Severinus of Noricum was a monk who appeared along the Danube after Attila's death (453), preaching and organizing relief among the ruined Roman provinces of Pannonia and Noricum; he died at Favianae on 8 January 482. He refused to speak of his origins, though he mentioned experience with eastern desert monasticism; his birthplace (Southern Italy or Africa) is speculation. Nearly everything known comes from Eugippius's Life (c. 511). Wace's Dictionary describes him as a stern ascetic and devoted missionary revered by Romans and barbarians alike; Odoacer sought him out for a blessing before invading Italy. He should not be confused with Severinus of Septempeda. Note: the sources describe this man as a missionary and wonder-worker, not as a writer; the doctrinal treatise held here under his name may be pseudepigraphal.
b.s: The single work held here, 'Doctrine' (PL 74), is an ascetic-moral instruction covering prayer, oaths, anger, silence, almsgiving, worship without holy places, and limits of forgiveness — teaching consistent with the eastern desert monasticism Severinus practiced.

b.bio: The library prints the name as Severus of Majorca; the sources identify him as Severus of Menorca (Minorca), a bishop on that island in the early fifth century. He is known from a single encyclical letter addressed to bishops, priests, deacons and all the brotherhood, describing how relics of St. Stephen deposited at Magona (Mahon) stirred religious excitement that ended in riots, the burning of the synagogue in January 418, and the conversion of some 540 Jews, including the rabbi Theodorus, defensor civitatis. Some scholars have attributed the letter to Consentius or doubted its authenticity; Blumenkranz dated it to the seventh century.
b.s: His one surviving work is the earliest document on the Church in Menorca and a key source for a Mediterranean Jewish community under Christian pressure in 418.

b.bio: Severus was bishop of Minorca in the early fifth century. In January 418, after relics of St. Stephen deposited at Magona by Orosius stirred religious excitement, disputes between Christians and the island's large Jewish community ended in riots in which the synagogue was burned; some 540 Jews converted within eight days, including the rabbi Theodorus, defensor civitatis. Severus reported these events in an encyclical letter to bishops, presbyters, and deacons throughout the world. Some historians have attributed the letter wholly or partly to Consentius, and a few scholars, notably Bernhard Blumenkranz, have dated it to the seventh century as a forgery.
b.s: The library holds his Epistle (PL 41), a firsthand account of coerced mass conversion that argues relics of martyrs kindle zeal, that zeal for Christ justifies attacking unbelievers, and that disputation with Jews must be honest rather than forced — a key document of early fifth-century Judeo-Christian polemic in the Mediterranean.

b.bio: Severus Rhetor is the name under which the library holds the bucolic poem printed in PL 19. The sources identify this author with Severus Sanctus Endelechius, a fourth-century Christian rhetorician and poet, probably of Gallic origin, who taught rhetoric at Rome — Sallustius's subscription to Apuleius records that he was a pupil there in 395 of the rhetorician Endelechius, declaiming in the forum of Mars. He was a friend of Paulinus of Nola, who dedicated his panegyric of Theodosius to him and credited him with the idea for it. The identification of 'Severus Rhetor' with Endelechius is reported by modern scholarship but remains a scholarly inference rather than a certainty.
b.s: His De mortibus boum (Carmen bucolicum de virtute signi crucis domini) is a rare piece of Christian apologetic cast in classical pastoral verse: against Bucolus's pagan grief and sacrifice, it argues that the sign of the cross protects from plague, that faith alone suffices for true worship, inward purity replacing blood sacrifice, and that Christ alone is God worthy of worship.

w: Fragment concerning the meaning of words

b.bio: Sextus Pompeius Festus was a Roman grammarian who probably flourished in the later 2nd century AD, perhaps at Narbo (Narbonne) in Gaul, though his date is disputed: Britannica places him in the 3rd century at Narbo, and Smith's Dictionary gives only that he lived after Martial and before Macrobius. He made an abridgment in twenty books, arranged alphabetically, of Marcus Verrius Flaccus's encyclopedic De verborum significatione, a work otherwise lost. He inserted critical remarks of his own, frequently correcting Verrius Flaccus, and removed obsolete words, treating them in a separate lost work, Priscorum verborum cum exemplis. Only one damaged manuscript of his epitome survives; the rest is known through Paul the Deacon's late-8th-century summary. The library holds two fragments from PL 95: the Fragment concerning the meaning of words and Notes.
b.s: His lexicon preserves, by quotation, Roman religious vocabulary and custom—numen (the nod and power of god), the temple as a place enclosed by augural formula, sacred tables standing in place of altars, mos as ancestral custom in religion—that would otherwise be lost, making it a primary source for Roman antiquities.

b.bio: Gaius Sollius Modestus Apollinaris Sidonius, born at Lyons on 5 November, about 430, into Gallo-Roman aristocracy, married Papianilla, daughter of the emperor Avitus, and served as urban prefect of Rome under Anthemius in 468. Elected bishop of Clermont around 469–470 against his wishes, he organized the city's defense against the Visigothic king Euric until its cession by treaty in 475, was imprisoned after the conquest but retained his see, and died in the early 480s (sources differ: Wikipedia gives 481/490, the Catholic Encyclopedia about August 480, Roman Letters 489, and ORB about 483). He is venerated as a saint with a feast day of 21 August.
b.s: His letters and poems are the principal surviving witness to the end of Roman Gaul from an insider's view — here including letters praising Theodoric II's civility while judging his Arian piety as custom rather than conviction, and opposing Euric and the Goths.

b.bio: Sigebert of Gembloux, a Benedictine monk born near Gembloux in Lower Lorraine around 1030–1035, taught at the Abbey of St. Vincent at Metz from about 1050 to 1070, then returned to Gembloux, where he ran the abbey school until his death on 5 October or 5 November 1112 (sources give both dates). He wrote saints' lives and poems for the houses whose relics they held — including a life of Bishop Theodoric I of Metz and a poem on St. Lucia for Metz, and works on the Theban Legion and the founder Wicbert for Gembloux. In the Investiture Controversy he became a partisan of Emperor Henry IV against Gregory VII, writing treatises against papal pretensions.
b.s: Best known as author of the Chronicon ab anno 381 ad 1113, a universal chronicle widely used by later medieval historians; the library holds only his short rhythms honoring Theodoric of Metz, which assert that pious acquisition of martyrs' relics honors God and that a bishop's holiness and generosity protect his city.

b.bio: The library prints this name for a Merovingian king of Austrasia, but two distinct figures bear it. The Sigebert II of the standard references (born 601/602, died late 613) was son of Theuderic II, placed on the throne by Brunhild, and killed by Chlotar II after a reign of weeks; he left no such acts. The letters held here instead cite Dagobert, Archbishop Modoald of Trier, and Bishop Principius of Speyer, matching the son of Dagobert I whom Butler's Lives treats under this name as a confessor-king. The record's works decide: this is Dagobert's son, whose dates The surviving records do not state.
b.s: The three pages in PL 87 are royal diplomas showing how Merovingian kingship exercised power through church endowment: grants of tolls and immunities to monasteries, tied to perpetual intercessory prayer.

w: Letters to Alexander II and Gregory VII

b.bio: Sigefrid of Mainz is Siegfried I, archbishop of Mainz from January 1060 until his death on 16 February 1084. Educated as a monk at Fulda, he was appointed abbot of Fulda on 25 December 1058 and appointed to Mainz by the Empress Agnes on 6 January 1060. He joined the faction of Anno II of Cologne after the Coup of Kaiserswerth (1062) and presided over the assembly of Worms in 1069. The letters held here are addressed to Popes Alexander II and Gregory VII and defend papal primacy and jurisdiction.
b.s: His letters are Gregorian-reform polemic from a leading German metropolitan: they assert Peter's primacy and the pope's universal pastoral office, require difficult cases to be referred to Rome, hold that synods need papal authorization for judgment, insist that inferior clergy owe obedience to the pope, and defend canonical episcopal consecration; they argue directly against King Henry IV, royal power, Bishop-designate Charles of Constance, and the murderers of Cuno of Trier.

w: On the Miracles of St. Maximinus

b.bio: Sigehard was a Benedictine monk of the royal abbey of St. Maximin in Trier, writing in the 960s under Ottonian rule. He is known for a single work, the Historia Miraculorum of St. Maximin, the fourth-century archbishop of Trier and patron of his monastery. The text records the saint's posthumous healing miracles and exorcisms, but also frames the period before a recent reform of the abbey as one of sin, using the saint's cult to justify that reform movement.
b.s: His Historia Miraculorum shows how a tenth-century monastic community used hagiography and recorded miracles to defend its reform and answer its critics.

w: Rhythm on the death of Fulk of Reims

b.bio: Sigloard of Reims appears in the sources only as a canon or monk of St-Remi in Reims around the year 900. His one attested work is a planctus — a lament in verse — on the death of Fulk, archbishop of Reims, in 900. The poem praises Fulk's adornment of the church, calls for the excommunication of his murderer and his abettors, and commends the dead bishop through mass and burial rites.
b.s: His lament on Fulk of Reims is both an elegy for a murdered archbishop and a polemic against Guinemarus, treating the church's judgment on the killer and prayer for the dead.

b.bio: Simpert was educated at Murbach Abbey in Alsace, where he took the Benedictine habit and was elected abbot. In 778 Charlemagne appointed him bishop of Augsburg; documents also style him bishop of Neuburg an der Donau (from 789) and of Neuburg im Staffelsee (from 800), while he remained abbot of Murbach. The Neuburg appointment was resigned in 802, and between 801 and 807 the diocese's territories east and west of the Lech were reunited under Augsburg alone. He rebuilt the Basilica of St Afra's, died 13 October 807, and was buried at St Afra's; his cultus was approved in 1468 (canonized 6 January 1468 by Pope Paul II). A tradition makes him a nephew of Charlemagne, but this is not established.
b.s: The works here are monastic legislation: statutes on regular life asserting that uncorrupted custom may stand as law, that all monks must practice lectio divina and labor with their own hands, and that abbots share the common table and fare of their brothers while guests are served worthily.

b.bio: Siviard was abbot of the monastery of Saint-Calais on the Anisole river in Maine, succeeding his own father Sigiram as head of the community, and died in 687 during the reign of Theuderic III according to the Sancteo notice. The dating is unsettled: the Sancteo notices label him a 7th-century abbot (while their own biographical text speaks of a birth in the first half of the 8th century), whereas the Migne edition titles him 'Siviardus V abbas Anisolensis' and dates the work to the 6th century (saeculo VI). He is known for one work, the Vita S. Carilefi (BHL 7799), written at episcopal command.
b.s: His Vita S. Carilefi presents the hermit's life as a model of self-denial, prayer, and anchoritic struggle that surpasses coenobitic perfection; it holds that saints' lives edify believers toward imitation and that their merits glorify God alone.

w: Preface to the Exposition of the Psalms

b.bio: A Benedictine monk, probably of Spanish (Visigothic) origin according to Wikipedia, though Encyclopedia.com suggests Irish origin; the disagreement is unresolved. He taught at Castellion, was elected abbot there about 805, and later moved his community to found Saint-Mihiel on the Meuse. Charlemagne employed him to draft the letter to Pope Leo III communicating the Council of Aachen's (809) decision on the filioque, and sent him to Rome with the delegation; Louis the Pious later used him as arbitrator in a dispute at Moyenmoutier. Sources differ on his death date: after 825 per Encyclopedia.com, about 840 per Wikipedia and Schaff.
b.s: His works here are homiletic collections on the Epistles and Gospels for the liturgical year, a commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict written for monastic reform, the Diadem of Monks drawn from the Fathers, and the Via regia on princely virtue addressed to Louis the Pious.

b.bio: Sonnatius was long archdeacon of the cathedral church of Reims, then succeeded Archbishop Romulus (in office 590–593) as its bishop. The Bollandists reconstruct his life from excerpts of Flodoard's Historia ecclesiae Remensis. He worked for the reform of church discipline and worship; in 613 he translated the relics of his forefather Remigius and gave him a costly tomb, and in 625 he presided over a council of more than forty bishops that reissued earlier disciplinary canons in twenty-five articles.
b.s: The Statutes held here are a pastoral-disciplinary text laying out sacramental teaching — grace conferred through rightly administered sacraments, confirmation, penance assigned to the pastor who knows his flock, Sunday mass attendance under penalty, marriage as an image of Christ and the church, extreme unction for the dying — in the tradition of Merovingian episcopal statutes.

w: Life of St. Mary of Egypt

b.bio:
Sophronius of Jerusalem (c. 560 – March 11, 638) — Sophronius was born in Damascus around 560, taught rhetoric, and became an ascetic in Egypt about 580 before entering the monastery of St. Theodosius near Bethlehem. He traveled with the chronicler John Moschus to monastic centers in Anatolia, Egypt, and Rome; Moschus dedicated his Pratum spirituale to him. As patriarch of Jerusalem from 634 until his death on March 11, 638, he led opposition to Monothelitism, addressed a Synodical Letter on Christ's two natures to the other patriarchs, and negotiated the surrender of Jerusalem to the caliph Umar in 637/8. He is venerated as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox and Catholic Churches.

Paul the Deacon (c. 796–799) — Paul the Deacon (Paulus Warnefridus) was born around the 720s at Cividale del Friuli to a noble Lombard family, son of Warnefrid and Theodelinda. He spent many years at the Lombard court in Pavia, serving as councillor under King Desiderius. After Charlemagne destroyed the Lombard kingdom he took refuge at Benevento with Duke Arichis II, became a Benedictine monk at Monte Cassino (ordained deacon c. 782), and was later brought to Charlemagne's court on account of his literary achievements before returning to Monte Cassino, where he died on 13 April in 796, 797, 798, or 799. He was a major contributor to the Carolingian Renaissance.
b.s: The library holds his Life of St. Mary of Egypt, a hagiographical narrative defending the reality of grace working miracles in every generation against readers inclined to disbelieve the account.

b.bio: Herrand was probably born in Swabia around 1040 into a prominent family of churchmen (his uncle was Burchard II of Halberstadt). Originally a monk of Gorze Abbey, he was sent to reform Saint Burchard's in Würzburg, served as schoolmaster of Halberstadt Cathedral, and by 1070 was abbot of Ilsenburg, where he reformed Saxon monasteries in the Gorze custom and helped re-establish Huysburg in 1076. After Burchard II's death in 1088 he was elected bishop of Halberstadt, but owing to the Investiture Contest could not enter the city, which was held by partisans of Emperor Henry IV. Pope Urban II consecrated him in Rome on 19 January 1094, where he took the name Stephen. In 1096 he established a provostry at Hillersleben subject to Ilsenburg, and around 1100 moved the Ilsenburg monks to Harsefeld Abbey for their safety. He took refuge in Magdeburg and later lived as a monk at Reinhardsbrunn Abbey, where he died on 23/24 October 1102.
b.s: The two works held here are historical commentaries from the Investiture Contest era, citing Dodechin, Berthold, and Valram, bishop of Magdeburg, and treating the Church, the civil magistrate, and the sacraments amid the conflict between Emperor Henry IV and his opponents.

w: Privilege granted to the proto-abbey of St. Martin

b.bio: Stephen, born Vajk at Esztergom around 975, was the son of Grand Prince Géza and the first Christian king of Hungary, crowned on 25 December 1000 or 1 January 1001 with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II (the Catholic Encyclopedia instead dates the coronation at Gran to 17 August 1001). He unified the Carpathian Basin against rival chieftains and pagan resistance, organized the Hungarian church under two archbishoprics (Esztergom and Kalocsa) and eight bishoprics, and founded monasteries and hospices. His only son Emeric died in a boar hunt on 2 September 1031; Stephen died on 15 August 1038 and was canonized at Székesfehérvár on 20 August 1083.
b.s: The works held here are his laws, his Admonitions to Prince Emeric, and a privilege to the abbey of St. Martin of Pannonhalma — documents in which a newly Christian kingdom legislates civil life by divine law and defines royal authority over church and property.

b.bio: Stephen III was born in Sicily around 720, son of a man named Olivus, and came to Rome under Gregory III. He became a Benedictine monk at St. Chrysogonus, was ordained priest under Zachary, and served at the Lateran Palace until his election as bishop of Rome on 1 August 768 (consecrated 7 August), amid the factional chaos following Paul I's death (which had produced the antipopes Constantine II and Philip). He held the see until his death on 24 January 772, summoned the Lateran Council of 769 against noble interference in papal elections and against iconoclasm, and corresponded with the Frankish kings Charlemagne and Carloman (sons of Pippin) and with the Lombard king Desiderius. Note on numbering: older catalogs (and Migne's PL 89 heading, followed by Documenta Catholica Omnia) date 'Stephanus III' letters to 752–757, conflating him with his predecessor Stephen (II) III; however, the content of the letters held here — addressed to King Carloman, King Desiderius, and Lord Pippin, and opposing Desiderius and the Lombards — belongs to the pontificate of 768–772.
b.s: The letters held here are papal correspondence from the crisis of the Lombard threat under Desiderius, appealing to the Frankish kings for the restoration of Peter's patrimony, arguing that prayers of intercession are owed to benefactors and that God rewards good works with heavenly recompense, and defending the Roman church against detractors such as Christopher and Sergius and against Lombard devastation.

w: From the Miracles of St. Modoald

b.bio: Stephen of Liège was born in the Low Countries around 850, educated at the cathedral school of Metz and then at Aachen's palace school from 864. He held abbacies at St Evre, St Mihiel and Lobbes and was a canon of Metz Cathedral before his election as bishop of Liège in 901. He died in Liège on 16 May 920. He was a hagiographer and composer; sources attribute to him Offices for the Holy Trinity, St Lambert and the Invention of St Stephen, though James Grier concludes Stephen had a hand in the Offices for St Lambert and the Trinity while the attribution of the Invention office remains uncertain. The works in this library are hagiographical: a Life of St Lambert and an account of miracles of St Modoald.
b.s: The works here defend relic cults and saintly intercession — chastity above temporal life, saints' prayers obtaining deliverance, saints interceding for their clients in heaven, burial near relics joining the dead to the saint — against those who despoiled shrines and against pagan invocation of nymphs and Mercury.

b.bio: Stephen of Senlis was archdeacon of Notre-Dame de Paris before his election as bishop of Paris in 1123, an office he held until his death on 6 May 1142. He was father of Guy, lord of Chantilly, descendant of the counts of Senlis. The works held here under 'Stephen of Paris' are his letters and diplomas from PL 173: correspondence in a dispute with Henry, archbishop of Sens, over the rights of a persecuted bishop, including appeals to the lord pope and Bernard of Clairvaux, together with charters of donation.
b.s: His letters are primary evidence for episcopal resistance to royal and metropolitan pressure in twelfth-century France, arguing that the liberty of the church must not be annihilated and that a wronged bishop may use interdict and joint appeal to Rome.

b.bio: The library's Stephanus VI is Pope Stephen (V) VI, bishop of Rome from September 885 until his death in September 891, a Roman aristocrat created cardinal-priest of SS. Quattro Coronati by Marinus I and consecrated without waiting for imperial confirmation from Charles the Fat. He crowned Guido III of Spoleto emperor in 891, recognized Louis the Blind as king of Provence, intervened in disputed episcopal elections such as Langres, and resisted the archbishops of Bordeaux and Ravenna and the attacks of Patriarch Photius. He must not be confused with the later pope also counted as Stephen VI (or VII), who reigned from 22 May 896 to August 897 and is remembered for the Cadaver Synod against Formosus; the numbering of these two pontiffs was long confused.
b.s: His letters in PL 129 are short acts of papal government: confirming property grants by apostolic authority, shielding churches from secular courts and tolls, asserting that episcopal election belongs to the local church rather than kings, providing for metropolitan oversight of suffragan elections, protecting monastic property via papal privilege, and anathematizing violations of papal privilege.

b.bio: A Roman, son of Teudemund (Theodemundus), and cardinal-priest of Sant'Anastasia before his election as pope in late 928 or early 929, during the period later called the Saeculum obscurum. His election was probably influenced by Marozia, whose family dominated Rome. His pontificate lasted about two years and is otherwise poorly documented; he died in February or March 931 and may have been assassinated. The sources number him Stephen VII or VIII depending on how an earlier Stephen is counted.
b.s: The library holds his letters and privileges for monasteries in France and Italy, which assert monastic exemption from local bishops under papal protection, free abbatial election by common consent, immunity from diocesan synods, and excommunication for violators of papal privileges.

b.bio: Stephen VIII was pope from 14 July 939 until his death in October 942. A Roman by birth and formerly cardinal-priest of SS. Silvester and Martin, he held office under the dominance of Alberic II of Spoleto and had little scope for independent action. His recorded interventions concern West Francia, where he backed King Louis IV against rebellious vassals under threat of excommunication, and monastic reform in the Cluniac line. The privileges printed in PL 132 under his name protect exempt monasteries from episcopal claims.
b.s: The letters and privileges held here are documents of papal protection for exempt Benedictine houses: they assert that apostolic authority shields monasteries from secular dominion, bar bishops of Pavia, Piacenza, Parma, and Reggio from a privileged house's tithes, allow free choice of consecrating bishop, and ground appeals by exempt abbots to the apostolic see in Peter's bind-and-loose power.

w: Sayings and Deeds of St. Stephen
Sayings and Deeds of St. Stephen of Muret

b.bio: Stephanus de Liciaco (also printed Stephanus de Liaciano; Stephen of Liac) was a prior of the Grandmontine order, active in the later twelfth century; Documenta Catholica Omnia dates him 1124–1192. He is not Stephen of Liège, the ninth-century bishop (d. 920), nor Stephen of Autun, the bishop and liturgical writer (d. 1139/1140). He wrote hagiography for his own order, most notably a Vita et Miracula of Stephen of Muret, the founder of Grandmont (BHL 7907), attributed to him 'ut videtur' according to the Légendiers latins database. The library holds this work as 'Sayings and Deeds of St. Stephen' in PL 204.
b.s: His Dicta et Facta preserves the sayings and ascetic teaching of Stephen of Muret, presenting the founder's renunciation of temporal goods, humility, love of God above all things, and deeds accompanying words as the pattern of Grandmontine sanctity.

w: Ancient customs of the Order of Saint Benedict
Order of the office in the house of St. Benedict

b.bio: Sturmius, a Bavarian by origin, was placed as a boy under Boniface and educated at the Benedictine monastery of Fritzlar. Ordained priest around 740, he worked as a missionary among the Hessians before Boniface commissioned him to found the monastery of Fulda on 12 March 744. He studied the organization of Subiaco, Monte Cassino, and St. Andrew's in 747–748, then served as Fulda's first abbot until his death there on 17 December 779. He was banished to Jumièges by Pepin in 763 over a dispute with Archbishop Lull of Mainz concerning Fulda's exemption, returning in 766. Charlemagne granted him part of the newly won Saxon lands as missionary territory. He was canonized in 1139.
b.s: The works held here are early Benedictine customary and liturgical material printed under his name in PL 89, prescribing monastic silence, forbidding swearing among monks, regulating prayer and labor, and detailing Holy Week observances such as the abbot's washing of feet on Maundy Thursday.

w: Statutes for the town of Saint-Sever

b.bio: Suavius appears in the library's record as abbot of Saint-Sever, the Gascon monastery whose statutes are printed under his name in PL 157. The statutes themselves invoke his authority, along with the founders of the monastery, an earlier abbot named Salvator, and the duke of Gascony and his wife Urraca. No surviving record gives dates for Suavius; the abbey's better-documented 11th-century abbots (Gregory of Montaner, abbot 1028–1072) belong to the same house but are not him. The sources describing Sulpicius Severus (c. 363–c. 425), the Aquitanian writer and biographer of St. Martin, concern a different person and are set aside.
b.s: The single work held here is a two-page set of town statutes for Saint-Sever, valuable as a record of how an abbot exercised lordship: gate-rights and tolls, criminal jurisdiction over homicide and theft, fixed fines, burgesses' attendance and military service, and market peace with rules for commerce outside the market.

w: On the Foundation of Westminster Abbey

b.bio: Sulcard was a Benedictine monk of St Peter's, Westminster Abbey, active around 1080. His entry into the monastery may date to the 1050s, and he may previously have been attached to the cathedral priory at Rochester, which receives attention in his work; his unusual name may reflect Anglo-Saxon or Norman parentage. His sole known work is the Prologus de construccione Westmonasterii, dedicated to Abbot Vitalis of Bernay (c. 1076–?1085), which he calls a 'commemorative book' (codex memorialis) for his house. A later Westminster chronicler, John Flete, records that Sulcard was buried in the cloister and that his remains were moved to the Chapter House when Henry III rebuilt the church.
b.s: He wrote the first history of Westminster Abbey, tracing its foundation from Mellitus's day through Edward the Confessor's new church and promoting the cult of St Peter as the abbey's miraculous patron.

b.bio: Sylvester I was bishop of Rome from 31 January 314 until his death on 31 December 335, the first pope to reign entirely under the liberty of the Church guaranteed by the Edict of Milan. The Liber pontificalis makes him the son of a Roman named Rufinus. His pontificate saw the Council of Arles (314) against the Donatists and the First Council of Nicaea (325), and the building of the Constantinian basilicas at Rome. Much that circulated under his name — the Vita beati Sylvestri, the Constitutum Sylvestri, and the Donation of Constantine — is apocryphal, and the works in PL 8 belong to this uncertain transmission.
b.s: The works held here are the small body of material printed under Sylvester's name in Migne's PL 8 — fragments on church unity, baptism, the uniform date of Easter, and the condemnation of the Donatists — documents for how the early Roman see was remembered and argued from.

b.bio: Gerbert of Aurillac, born near Aurillac in Auvergne around 945–950, trained at the monastery there and in Spain under Arabian teachers before teaching at Reims. He held the abbey of Bobbio from Otto II in 983, aided Hugh Capet's accession, became pope on 2 April 999, and died in Rome on 12 May 1003. The works held here are papal letters and decrees confirming monastic privileges: they defend free election of abbots by monks, bar alienation of monastic property without papal confirmation, extend ecclesiastical immunity against lay and episcopal molestation, and anathematize violators — including Stephen, invader of the church of Le Puy; Azelin of Laon; and the bishop of Autun.
b.s: The letters here show a tenth-century pope asserting papal privilege as the guarantor of monastic liberty against local bishops and lay powers.

b.bio:
Synod of Mainz (unknown) — The library's single item under this name is a short set of acts from a synod held at Mainz, in which Sigefrid, primate of Mainz, is cited by name. The acts belong to the era of conflict between King Henry IV and the reform papacy: they condemn simoniacally invested bishops, declare that papal authority outranks royal power in church matters, cite Hildebrand (Gregory VII), and argue against Charles of Constance and the royal court of Henry IV.

Siegfried of Mainz (d. 16 February 1084) — Siegfried I was educated at Fulda and became a monk there, its abbot from 25 December 1058 to 6 January 1060, when Empress Agnes appointed him Archbishop of Mainz; he held that see until his death on 16 February 1084. A member of the Frankish Reginbodonen family of the Rhineland, he joined Anno II of Cologne's faction after the Coup of Kaiserswerth (1062) and presided over the assembly of Worms in 1069, at which Henry IV announced his intent to repudiate Bertha. The library holds a single short text under his name: three pages of acts (PL 148) concerning the bishopric of Constance.
b.s: The acts are a compact witness to Gregorian-reform polemic in Germany, asserting papal supremacy over royal power and purging simony from the episcopate.

b.bio:
Synod held in Gaul (unknown) — The library holds under this name two pages of acts from a synod in Gaul concerning the abbey of Cluny and its dispute with Drogo, bishop of Mâcon. The acts reserve Cluny to the Roman pontiff alone, assert that apostolic privileges secure monastic liberty against episcopal excommunication, and rule that unwitting breach of those privileges requires oath satisfaction. The text cites Peter Damian, Abbot Hugh of Cluny, Count William, Pope Agapetus, and Pope Alexander. None of The surviving records describe this synod; they concern Reticius of Autun, Vincent of Lérins, the Synod of Arles, and Gregory of Tours, which belong to different persons and centuries and cannot be used for this author.

Peter Damian (c. c. 1007–1073) — Born in or around 1007 at Ravenna, Peter Damian took his surname from his brother Damianus, an archpriest there who had him educated after a neglected childhood. He studied and taught at Ravenna, Faenza, and Parma, then about 1035 entered the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, where he became prior. He joined the reforming circle of Pope Leo IX, was made Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia, and worked for the Gregorian Reform against simony and clerical incontinence. He died at Faenza on 21 February 1072; some sources give 1073.
b.s: The acts here are a brief documentary witness to a conflict between Cluniac exemption and episcopal jurisdiction.

b.bio: Sebastian Tengnagel was born in Büren in Geldern; sources disagree on the year, giving either 1563 or 1573, and he died in Vienna on 4 April 1636. A doctor of both laws, he served as imperial librarian at the Hofbibliothek in Vienna, where he built the library's first major collection of Arabic, Turkish, Persian, and Hebrew manuscripts, and also sat as a councillor and presided over the Viennese Senate. His Counter-Reformation commitments shaped his scholarship: the work held here assembles old documents defending Gregory VII, Alexander III, and Adrian IV against schismatics and their calumniators.
b.s: The works here are his Vetera Monumenta Contra Schismaticos, a polemical citation-survey marshalling Tertullian, Baronius, and Callimachus to defend medieval popes from calumny and assert the Roman church's apostolic foundation.

b.bio: Stephan Alexander Würdtwein was born in Amorbach; most sources give 1719, though Catholic-Hierarchy gives 12 October 1722 (day uncertain), so the birth year remains disputed. He studied philosophy, theology and canon law at Heidelberg (1738–1743), then canon law and dogma at Mainz, and was ordained a priest in 1745 (sources differ on the exact day: 18 July per English Wikipedia, 18 December per Catholic-Hierarchy). After a chaplaincy in Bingen and a benefice at Werbach he served the Electorate of Mainz under three archbishops as a historian and church administrator, and on 18 July 1783 was appointed Auxiliary Bishop of Worms with the titular see of Heliopolis in Augustamnica. He died in Ladenburg on 11 April 1796.
b.s: The two pieces held here are his editorial prefaces to the Boniface materials in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 89, where he dates Boniface's mission to 716 (supported by Boniface's letter to Zachary), defends that date against the Würzburg chronicle and Peter the Librarian, and records the martyrdom of 755.

b.bio: Severian was bishop of Gabala in Syria who came to Constantinople around 400 and won fame as a preacher despite a strong Syrian accent. Chrysostom entrusted him with the care of the Constantinopolitan church during his journey to Asia in 401, but conflict with the deacon Serapion turned Severian against Chrysostom; he became a favourite of Empress Eudoxia and helped condemn Chrysostom at the Synod of the Oak. Gennadius praises him as learned in Scripture and admirable as a homilist. More than fifty sermons survive, many transmitted under Chrysostom's name.
b.s: Remembered chiefly as a popular Antiochene preacher and principal opponent of John Chrysostom; the library holds his baptismal homilies from PG 65, which argue that Christ sanctifies the baptismal waters rather than being sanctified by them, and that the Trinity manifested at Christ's baptism.

b.bio: Synesius was born of a wealthy family at Balagrae near Cyrene between 370 and 375. He studied at Alexandria under the philosopher Hypatia and became a committed Neoplatonist, remaining her correspondent for life. In 398 the Pentapolis sent him as envoy to Constantinople to seek tax relief from Arcadius; there he delivered De regno, urging war on corruption and on barbarians in the army. After years as a country gentleman he was made bishop of Ptolemais after 410, accepting office while keeping his philosophical convictions.
b.s: The works held here — above all the Letters and On Providence — show a Christian bishop writing as a Greek gentleman-philosopher, treating providence, kingship, dreams, and church discipline in Attic prose that cites Homer and Plato more than any Christian authority.

b.bio: Stephen I was Bishop of Rome from 12 May 254 until his death on 2 August 257; according to the most ancient catalogues he was born in Rome and was son of Jovius, and he served as archdeacon under Lucius I, who designated him his successor. His pontificate is known chiefly through the letters of Cyprian of Carthage. He defended the validity of baptism administered by heretics against Cyprian and the African and Asian bishops who demanded rebaptism, holding that converts should be received by the laying on of hands. He also restored two Spanish bishops accused of apostasy in the Decian persecution.
b.s: His refusal to require rebaptism of heretics fixed the Roman position in the controversy with Cyprian and Firmilian and shaped later sacramental theology on baptismal validity.

b.bio: Frederick of Lorraine, of the Ardenne-Verdun ducal family and brother of Duke Godfrey the Bearded of Lorraine, was a canon at Liège before his cousin Leo IX made him chancellor and librarian of the Roman Church around 1051. He served as papal legate to Constantinople in 1054, entered Monte Cassino as a monk in 1055, became its abbot in 1057, and was made cardinal-priest of St. Chrysogonus by Victor II shortly before succeeding him as pope on 3 August 1057. His eight-month pontificate continued Leo IX's reform program; he died at Florence on 29 March 1058. Sources give his birth year variously as c. 1000 or c. 1020.
b.s: Bishop of Rome for an eight-month pontificate, continuing Leo IX's reform program until his death at Florence on 29 March 1058. His letters defend papal privilege, apostolic jurisdiction, and clerical exemption from secular judgment and tribute.
